blocks.docstring:
**Rota's basis conjecture.** Let $M$ be a matroid of rank $n$ and let $B_1, \dots, B_n$ be
$n$ pairwise disjoint bases of $M$. Then the elements of these bases can be arranged into an
$n \times n$ matrix whose $i$-th row consists exactly of the elements of $B_i$ and each of whose
columns is also a base of $M$.

Equivalently, there are $n$ disjoint bases $C_1, \dots, C_n$ of $M$ (the columns), each of which
consists of exactly one element from each of the bases $B_i$.

The matrix is a function `A : Fin n → Fin n → α`, with `i`-th row `A i` and `j`-th column
`fun i ↦ A i j`. The rank of `M` is `Matroid.eRank : ℕ∞`, so `M.eRank = n` says that every base
of `M` has exactly `n` elements. Hence `Set.range (A i) = B i` says that the `i`-th row lists the
elements of `B i` without repetition. The case `n = 0` is trivially true.

claims.decomposer_note: Universally quantified over all n and all matroids M of (finite) rank n with n pairwise disjoint bases B_1,...,B_n; the conclusion is the existence of a bijective n×n arrangement (equivalently n disjoint 'transversal' bases C_1,...,C_n, each containing exactly one element of every B_i) whose row i is exactly B_i and every column is a base of M — the vector-space form in the article is just the linear-matroid special case, and the partial results (paving matroids, n ≤ 3, Ω(√n) columns, Alon–Tarsi implication) and the Bárány–Larman colored Tverberg conjecture are background, not questions the statement poses; n = 0 is a trivially true boundary case.
claims.reviewer_why: All eight candidates state the same mathematically equivalent, faithful formalization (∀ α, n, M with M.eRank = n, pairwise disjoint bases B : Fin n → Set α; ∃ A : Fin n → Fin n → α with Set.range (A i) = B i for each row and M.IsBase (Set.range fun i ↦ A i j) for each column). Chose c08 for the cleanest form: plain function (not Matrix, whose entries need not be ring elements), hypotheses as binders, standard `Pairwise fun i j ↦ Disjoint (B i) (B j)` idiom, no redundant injectivity clauses (row injectivity is provable from range equality since bases have exactly n elements — verified in a scratch proof via IsBase.encard_eq_eRank and Finite.injOn_of_encard_image_eq), and a docstring that explains this. Edits: copyright year updated to 2026 (repo's current year), references section and docstring lightly tightened.

context: In linear algebra and matroid theory, Rota's basis conjecture is an unproven conjecture concerning rearrangements of bases, named after Gian-Carlo Rota. It states that, if X is either a vector space of dimension n or more generally a matroid of rank n, with n disjoint bases Bi, then it is possible to arrange the elements of these bases into an n × n matrix in such a way that the rows of the matrix are exactly the given bases and the columns of the matrix are also bases. That is, it should be possible to find a second set of n disjoint bases Ci, each of which consists of one element from each of the bases Bi.

decomposition_objections.text: None. The single slot captures the whole list entry, and the notes' reading (universally quantified over n and finite-rank matroids; conclusion is a bijective n×n arrangement with rows Bᵢ and base columns; n = 0 trivial) is what the file states.

/--
**Rota's basis conjecture.** Let $M$ be a matroid of rank $n$ and let $B_1, \dots, B_n$ be
$n$ pairwise disjoint bases of $M$. Then the elements of these bases can be arranged into an

@[category research open, AMS 5 15]
theorem rotas_basis_conjecture {α : Type*} (n : ℕ) (M : Matroid α) (hM : M.eRank = n)
    (B : Fin n → Set α) (hB : ∀ i, M.IsBase (B i))
    (hdisj : Pairwise fun i j ↦ Disjoint (B i) (B j)) :
    ∃ A : Fin n → Fin n → α,
      (∀ i, Set.range (A i) = B i) ∧ ∀ j, M.IsBase (Set.range fun i ↦ A i j) := by
  sorry

end RotasBasisConjecture

items: Rank n is expressed as `M.eRank = (n : ℕ∞)` (Mathlib's extended-natural rank; there is no ℕ-valued `Matroid.rank` in this Mathlib version). Equality with a natural number n forces finite rank, and then every base has exactly n elements (`IsBase.encard_eq_eRank`).

No finiteness of the ground set is assumed (Mathlib matroids may be infinite). The source says only 'matroid of rank n'. The finite-rank statement with an infinite ground set is equivalent to the finite-matroid statement: restrict M to the finite set ⋃ Bᵢ; the Bᵢ remain bases, and any base of the restriction has n elements so is a base of M.
The n × n matrix is modelled as `A : Fin n → Fin n → α` rather than Mathlib's `Matrix`, since entries are arbitrary matroid elements, not ring elements. Row i is `A i`, column j is `fun i => A i j`.

The condition 'rows are Bᵢ' is `Set.range (A i) = B i`. Because `B i` is a base of a rank-n matroid it has exactly n elements, so a surjection from `Fin n` onto it is automatically a bijection; injectivity was checked in a scratch proof and is not stated redundantly.

The condition 'columns are also bases' is `M.IsBase (Set.range fun i => A i j)`. Since `A i j ∈ B i` and the `B i` are pairwise disjoint, each column has exactly one element from each `B i`, and distinct columns are automatically disjoint, matching the article's equivalent formulation with n disjoint 'transversal' bases Cⱼ.
Disjointness of the bases is `Pairwise fun i j => Disjoint (B i) (B j)` on `Fin n` (i.e. for all i ≠ j), the idiom used elsewhere in the repository.
n = 0 is permitted and trivially true (empty family, empty matrix), as the decomposition notes indicate.

Only the matroid form is stated; the vector-space form is the linear-matroid special case and the partial results/related conjectures are background, per the decomposition notes. No bespoke definitions were needed.
AMS tags 5 (combinatorics: matroids) and 15 (linear algebra), matching the 'algebra' tag and the matroid setting.

references.title: Optimal bounds for the colored Tverberg problem

reviewer_notes: The statement quantifies over all Mathlib matroids (possibly infinite ground set) of finite rank n; this is equivalent to the finite-matroid form since the conjecture only concerns the finite set ⋃ B_i. `M.eRank = (n : ℕ∞)` is the only available rank notion in this Mathlib (no ℕ-valued Matroid.rank); it forces every base to have exactly n elements, which in turn makes `Set.range (A i) = B i` a bijective enumeration and makes columns automatically consist of one element from each B_i and be pairwise disjoint — matching the article's equivalent 'transversal bases C_j' phrasing. n = 0 is allowed and trivially true (checked with a one-line proof). Candidates c01/c02/c05 added redundant injectivity clauses (harmless); c03/c06 used `Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) α` (harmless but stylistically odd for non-ring entries); c03/c07 added extra non-slot variants (vector-space form, n ≤ 3 solved case, n = 0 test) which I did not ship since the task is to output exactly the surviving slots. No candidate omitted the slot; no decomposition objections were raised and I agree with the decomposition.
